extracted.intended_audience: public relations counsels, students, and practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and practical criteria for planning and executing public-relations campaigns: how to select media, segment and appeal to publics, time messages, and work within social/psychological limits on persuasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared fundamentals between cause and public
rubrics_metrics.description: The cause he represents must have some group reaction and tradition in common with the public he is trying to reach. This must exist before they can react sympathetically upon one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If common fundamentals do not exist, sympathy cannot be manufactured; the counsel can only intensify or dissipate existing sympathy. Examples: Margaret Sanger evokes enthusiasm where audiences already approve; prison reform speech during a crime wave finds little response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limitations of PR effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: The public relations counsel must continually realize that there are always these limitations to his effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaders and preachers live with their ears to the ground; sympathy between orator and audience cannot be created from thin air. Counsel should avoid claims that PR 'manufactures' public opinion and instead work within existing predispositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use established mediums of communication
rubrics_metrics.description: The public can be reached only through established mediums of communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Innovators cannot generally create their own channels; counsel must utilize the daily press, magazines, lecture circuits, advertising mediums, motion picture channels, radio, etc. This is both a limitation and an opportunity—existing channels give credibility and access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subdivide appeals and present through many avenues
rubrics_metrics.description: The public relations counsel must always sub-divide the appeal of his subject and present it through the widest possible variety of avenues to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segment the audience and tailor approaches for each segment rather than a single mass appeal. Example campaigns: charity organizers forming groups of dentists, bankers, theatrical owners; railroads using posters to awaken basic instincts of care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage interlapping group formations
rubrics_metrics.description: Society consists of many interlapping groups; the counsel utilizes these overlapping memberships to reach individuals by multiple appeals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze component groups and appeal to each on its strongest ground. Example: silk firm addressed women as members of museums (art), women's clubs (fashion), schools (education), and newspapers (news). Use overlapping ties to multiply exposure and reinforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for heterogeneity of modern audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Populations have increased and become heterogeneous; groups lack common ancestry or traditions, making it necessary to reach totally dissimilar groups as to ideals, customs and language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume homogeneity; craft messages and select channels that can reach diverse subgroups (urban/rural, educated/uneducated, different ethnicities). Example: U.S. Steel having to present views to employees of varied origins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and public readiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Public response depends on whether the public is prepared to meet the message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose moments when public sentiment is receptive (Madam Curie example). A message delivered at an inopportune time (e.g., prison reform during a crime wave) will find little response; successful counsel times appeals to public readiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit changed external conditions and new media
rubrics_metrics.description: Changed physical conditions and technologies (radio, automobile, airplane) create new possibilities and require new estimates of viewpoint change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how new media change public perceptions and use them to reach larger audiences; also consider how promoting a new technology can accelerate its adoption (e.g., manufacturers of radio enlarging radio's field).

rubrics_metrics.name: Find and appeal to the greatest common factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity can be secured only by finding the greatest common factor or divisor of all the groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When aiming for broad acceptance, base appeals on fundamental, widely shared values (loyalty, fairness, patriotism) rather than narrow interests. Example: appeals to employers and returned soldiers emphasized loyalty and fairness for reëstablishing ex-service men.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present new facts in accustomed ways
rubrics_metrics.description: People accept the facts which come to them through existing channels. They like to hear new things in accustomed ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame and package novel information so it fits familiar formats and channels—readers have neither time nor inclination to search for unfamiliar sources. Using familiar presentation increases uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer existing channels due to cost and feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern conditions make it not feasible to build up independent organs; establishing new newspapers, radio stations, or film distribution is difficult, slow and costly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess resource requirements and cost-effectiveness before attempting new channels; often better to leverage established press and media rather than create expensive new organs (text cites high startup and operating costs for newspapers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt the perspective of an impartial observer
rubrics_metrics.description: The training of the public relations counsel permits him to step out of his own group to look at a particular problem with the eyes of an impartial observer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counsel must use knowledge of individual and group psychology rather than personal biases, so as to project the client's point of view accurately to the target publics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use gradual change via intergroup interplay rather than abrupt upheaval
rubrics_metrics.description: Progress seldom occurs through abrupt expulsion of old ideas; it comes through rearrangement of individuals' thoughts across interlapping groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for incremental shifts by leveraging cross-cutting identities and slow persuasion rather than revolutionary messaging; exploit the inconstancy and multiple group commitments of individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate internal censorship and 'logic-proof compartments'
rubrics_metrics.description: The average citizen is the world’s most efficient censor. His own mind is the greatest barrier between him and the facts—his 'logic-proof compartments' and absolutism prevent him from seeing in terms of experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design messages that overcome cognitive and social censorship by framing, repetition, and presenting information via trusted channels; propaganda is a directed effort to overcome the censorship of the group mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor message framing to subgroup dominant interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Each subgroup should be appealed to on the basis of its greatest interest and presented accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame the same product or idea differently for different segments (e.g., silk as fashion for women's clubs, as art for museum-goers, as natural history for schools). Select the dominant appeal for each subgroup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate multi-channel campaigns for reinforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: Utilize many types of appeal and many mediums to increase reach and reinforce the message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine posters, advertising, news coverage, lectures, and other channels to reach large and diverse publics; multiple exposures via different appeals increase probability of response (e.g., Russian Ballet reached art lovers, music lovers, and general public through varied appeals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess and plan according to resource constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: The cost and logistics of building and maintaining media outlets are substantial and must shape strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate capital and operating costs (newspaper creation, radio station, film distribution) and choose strategies that are proportionate and sustainable; many new ventures fail or run at loss for long periods.
